gap.reason: The introduction emphasizes the need to overcome inadequate friction and wear performance, particularly the thermal instability of existing solid lubricants, by designing self-lubricating composites for wide-temperature operation.

source_text:
The rapid development of aerospace, nuclear industries, and new energy vehicles demands effective lubrication and wear control for critical moving components, as these directly determine the performance and operational lifespan of machinery. Achieving a low coefficient of friction (COF) and wear rates (WR) under extreme conditions such as high temperature, heavy load, and irradiation environments remains a persistent challenge in tribology. Solid lubricants can effectively separate surfaces while providing lubrication and wear resistance. However, most solid lubricants suffer from thermal instability at elevated temperatures: graphite undergoes oxidative decomposition above 450 °C and MoS2 transforms into non-lubricious MoO3 beyond 500 °C. Therefore, lubricant hybridization and tribochemically modified compositions offer promising approaches for extreme conditions such as wide-temperature-range operation.

Mo, Ag, and MoS2 are often used as additives in composites. These additives can form lubricating oxides and molybdates such as MoO3 and Ag2MoO4 on the worn surfaces of composites at elevated temperatures. Hector Torres et al. investigated the high-temperature lubrication properties of various oxides and molybdates and found that MoO3 (0.20), NiMoO4 (0.29) and Ag2MoO4 (0.28) exhibit low COF at 704 °C. Wang et al. studied the tribological behavior of Ni3Al-Ag based self-lubricating alloys in a wide temperature range and revealed a wear mechanism in which Ag provides lubrication at lower temperatures, while tribochemically generated NiO and Ag2MoO4 contribute to friction reduction at higher temperatures. The combination of Ag and Ag2MoO4 exerts a synergistic effect, enabling excellent lubrication over a broad temperature range. Enkang Hao et al. examined the high-temperature tribological characteristics of NiCoCrAlYTa/Ag/Mo coatings and demonstrated that the outward diffusion and oxidation of Ag and Mo at high temperatures lead to the formation of a continuous β-Ag2MoO4 lubricating film on the coating surface. Meanwhile, minor hard particles such as NiO within the coating effectively bear the load during friction, resulting in optimal tribological performance of the composite coating. Considering the lubricating oxides and molybdates formed on worn surfaces under high-temperature conditions, it is of great significance to pre-design self-lubricating composites to control the high-temperature friction and wear performance.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are novel alloy systems with outstanding properties demonstrating considerable potential in practical applications. Research on CoCrFeNi HEAs has mainly focused on their microstructure, mechanical properties, and oxidation resistance, while investigations into their tribological performance over a wide temperature range remain limited. Zhang et al. fabricated two distinct CoCrFeNi-based self-lubricating composites via spark plasma sintering (SPS). Their study revealed that the composites exhibit excellent mechanical properties and favorable friction and wear performance from room temperature (RT) to 800 °C, which is attributed to the synergistic effects among the HEA matrix, solid lubricant phases, and various metal oxides generated on the worn surface through tribochemical reactions.

queries.broad: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.
queries.problem_constrained: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.
queries.expert_context: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Conventional solid lubricants have limited high-temperature stability: graphite oxidatively decomposes above 450 °C, while MoS2 becomes non-lubricious MoO3 beyond 500 °C. Earlier composite studies used Mo-, Ag-, and MoS2-containing additives and reported temperature-dependent lubrication associated with Ag and tribochemically generated oxides or molybdates; CoCrFeNi-based composites produced by spark plasma sintering also showed favorable performance up to 800 °C. Nevertheless, wide-temperature tribological research on CoCrFeNi remains limited, and any solution must retain effectiveness despite the changing processes that occur from room to elevated temperature. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

Discloses Ag-mediated lubrication, which is part of the answer's low-to-medium-temperature mechanism.

Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges.
